Clear write deadline after frame ping to fix HTTP/2 stream failure (#588)

The data write path (writeData) clears the write deadline after each write,
including the extra NetConn().SetWriteDeadline clear required on HTTP/2 where
an expired deadline cannot be extended by a later write. The frame ping path
armed the same deadline via WriteControl but never cleared it.

With frame ping-pong enabled over a WebSocket carried on HTTP/2, the ping set
a short (writeTimeout) deadline on the underlying connection and left it. Once
it expired, the next write (a data message or the following ping) could not
re-arm the deadline and the stream failed permanently. Plain HTTP/1 connections
were unaffected.

Extract the clear into clearWriteDeadline and call it on both paths.

Disable automatic read op retries in Redis (#591)

Centrifuge issues Redis commands without per-request context deadlines
and relies on IOTimeout to bound every call: when Redis is unreachable,
callers expect an error within roughly the IOTimeout envelope. Writes
and Lua scripts already behaved that way — they are not retried by
rueidis and fail on the first attempt.

Read-only commands did not. rueidis retries them on network errors
until the context is done, and with context.Background() that means
never: a presence-style read issued during a Redis outage kept
retrying (a burst of near-immediate attempts, then roughly once per
second) and simply did not return until Redis came back or the client
was closed.

Disable client-level retries entirely so reads fail the same way
writes do. Centrifuge surfaces errors to its callers, which own their
retry semantics; silently masking transient errors inside the client
is not a behavior anything relies on. Both the main and the replica
client inherit the setting since they share one ClientOption.

The test builds a shard through a local TCP proxy, stops the proxy to
produce the same errors a crashed Redis gives (broken connections,
refused dials), and requires a deadline-less GET to fail within
seconds. Without DisableRetry it retries against the dead address and
never returns.

Redis keepalive bound (#592)

Centrifuge issues Redis commands without per-request context deadlines
and promises callers that commands fail within a bounded time when
Redis is unreachable. For a connection that stalls silently — the peer
stops replying while TCP stays open (frozen server, partition without
resets) — no write deadline fires, and the only rescue is the rueidis
keepalive: after Dialer.KeepAlive of reply silence it sends a PING
bounded by ConnWriteTimeout, and the PING failure tears the connection
down, erroring every pending command.

The worst case is 2*KeepAlive + IOTimeout: a straggler reply can make
one keepalive tick look active, only the next tick sends the PING, and
the PING waits a full IOTimeout. With the rueidis default KeepAlive of
1s and the default 4s IOTimeout that is 6 seconds. Set KeepAlive to
400ms so the worst case stays within 5 seconds (4.8s with defaults).

The test reproduces the silent stall with a TCP proxy that switches
into blackhole mode (connections stay open, nothing is forwarded) and
requires a pending command to fail within the formula bound — it
observes the predicted worst case almost exactly (2.79s with a 2s
IOTimeout). Without a working keepalive the same command hangs
indefinitely. The test warms every multiplexed wire first: commands
landing on a wire created after the stall began measure the fresh
handshake instead, which is separately bounded by ConnectTimeout.

Close transport before per-channel cleanup on disconnect (#595)

* Close transport before per-channel cleanup on disconnect

Presence removal and the leave PUBLISH in the unsubscribe loop are synchronous
PresenceManager/Broker round trips. Running them before transport.Close means
that under load (slow Redis) the socket teardown is gated behind them: the old
connection lingers on the server while a reconnecting client that already timed
out opens a new one, producing several concurrent connections per client
(centrifuge-js#371).

Reorder close() so removeClient, the disconnect push and transport.Close run
first, then the per-channel cleanup. None of the cleanup writes to the transport,
and it still runs under presenceMu with c.closing set, so the presence-tick
coordination is unaffected. OnUnsubscribe still fires before OnDisconnect.

Because the transport is now torn down before the cleanup loop, hub subscription
state converges shortly after the transport close signal rather than strictly
before it; TestHubDisconnect waits for convergence accordingly.

* Keep disconnect teardown clear of presence round trips

Two follow-ups to closing the transport before the per-channel cleanup.

A closing connection stays registered in the hub subscription shards until
the cleanup loop reaches each channel, so publications keep being routed to
it after the writer is closed. Every one of them fails to enqueue, and the
broadcast path answered that by spawning a close() goroutine that had
nothing to do but block until the in-flight close finished - one goroutine
per message per closing connection, worst exactly when the cleanup (and so
the window) is slowest. Skip the spawn when a close is already running.

close() also took presenceMu before doing anything. The cleanup does need
it - it removes presence entries and must not overlap a tick that is still
adding them - but taking it up front put an in-flight tick's PresenceManager
round trip, or its timeout, in front of transport.Close, keeping the socket,
the hub entry and the inflight-connections gauge alive for the duration.
Take presenceMu only for the cleanup. Only close() takes both mutexes, so
the connectMu -> presenceMu order cannot invert against anything else.

Both are covered by regression tests that fail with their fix reverted.

Fix nil pointer panic when delta publication fails JSON encoding (#597)

getDeltaData took jsonEncodeErr as *encodeError and wrote through it with
*jsonEncodeErr = encodeError{...}, but broadcastPublication passes its own
nil *encodeError. A JSON encode failure on the delta path therefore
dereferenced nil and panicked the broadcasting goroutine. Nothing in the
library recovers, so the panic reaches the broker PUB/SUB consumer and
terminates the process.

The same call also had a second, quieter defect: writing to the pointee
rather than rebinding the caller's variable meant the caller's
`jsonEncodeErr != nil` check could never fire, so the offending client
would never be disconnected even if the panic had not occurred.

Take **encodeError instead, matching what the non-delta paths already do
with `jsonEncodeErr = &encodeError{...}`. Both defects go away: the
broadcast survives and the client is disconnected with
DisconnectInappropriateProtocol, exactly as on the non-delta path.

Reaching this needs a JSON subscriber with Fossil delta active and a
publication whose encoding fails. Publication.Data cannot be the trigger
(it is always json.Escape'd for JSON+Fossil), but ClientInfo.ConnInfo and
ChanInfo are embedded raw and the encoder validates the whole assembled
document, so application-supplied info that is not valid JSON reaches it.
Protobuf subscribers and non-delta JSON subscribers were unaffected.

Remove per-drain allocation from the broadcast fan-out path (#598)

Profiling a 1000-subscriber broadcast showed one allocation per drain per
connection, all from a single line: make([]Item, 0, count) in
queue.RemoveMany, reached from writer.waitSendMessage when writeDelay == 0.
The writeDelay > 0 path already drained into a pooled buffer via
getItemBuf + RemoveManyInto; the default path did not.

Use the pooled buffer in both. Draining goes through a new
queue.RemoveManyIntoShrink, which removes and shrinks in one critical
section, so both the shrink timing and the lock traffic match the
RemoveMany call it replaces. Two details this preserves that a
FinishCollect-based version would not: QueueShrinkDelay stays inert when
WriteDelay is zero (as documented), and the queue mutex - contended by
every broadcast producer - is still taken once per drain rather than
twice. A test pins the equivalence against RemoveMany across cap/fill/
drain combinations, comparing length, size, capacity and FIFO order.

Two smaller costs in the same path:

- broadcastPublication, broadcastJoin and broadcastLeave looked up
  prepared payloads in a map keyed by a struct holding a string, hashing
  it once per subscriber, and allocated that map per broadcast. Nearly
  every channel has a single protocol/delta/useID/filtered combination,
  so a one-entry front cache serves every subscriber after the first and
  the map is only built when a channel really does mix combinations.
  subInfo now also snapshots the transport's protocol type and
  unidirectional flag at addSub time - both are fixed for the connection's
  lifetime, but reading them cost two interface dispatches per subscriber
  per broadcast.

- observeBroadcastDuration was the only metric helper resolving its
  histogram child on every call. It now caches by label set like its
  siblings. The cache key carries both declared labels, not just the
  namespace, so a future second call site cannot silently get the wrong
  child. Its duplicated if/else branches were identical; dropped.

Measured with the added benchmarks, interleaved A/B, benchstat n=6, all
p=0.002:

  Broadcast_1000Subs         1000 -> 9.5 allocs/op   -99.1%   B/op -95.3%
  BroadcastOffset_1000Subs   1001 -> 4.5 allocs/op   -99.6%   B/op -98.8%
  BroadcastMixedProtocol     1001 -> 5.5 allocs/op   -99.5%   B/op -96.5%
  Broadcast_100Subs            95 -> 3.5 allocs/op   -96.3%   B/op -89.3%
  ManyChannels                  9 -> 6   allocs/op   -33.3%   B/op -28.9%
  geomean                             allocs -93.9%, bytes -86.8%

Broadcast_1Sub is unchanged at 2 allocs/op, as expected: with a single
subscriber the writer drains one item per batch either way and there is

Default QueueShrinkDelay so batching writers stop rebuilding their queue (#600)

A connection with WriteDelay enabled and QueueShrinkDelay left at its zero
value allocated on every write cycle: 84 allocs and 34KB per publication
broadcast to 200 subscribers.

The shrink decision is taken from FinishCollect immediately after a drain,
when the queue is empty by construction. doShrinkLocked then halves while
cnt <= k && k >= initCap, and with cnt == 0 that always walks the whole way
down to QueueInitialCap (2). So each cycle discarded the ring the writer had
just filled, and the next frame rebuilt it one doubling at a time
(2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16). The policy was reading utilisation at the trough of a
sawtooth, where for a batching writer it is always zero.

QueueShrinkDelay already solves this - a non-zero delay defers the decision,
and under sustained load the timer keeps resetting so the queue simply
settles at its working set. The problem was purely that its zero value meant
"shrink immediately", making the default the pathological setting for exactly
the users who enable WriteDelay. Both are PRO options and the coupling was
only discoverable by reading both doc comments.

Treat zero as unset and apply DefaultQueueShrinkDelay. A negative value now
selects immediate shrinking, kept for completeness though it only
reintroduces the churn. The no-WriteDelay path never reaches FinishCollect
and is untouched.

Broadcast to 200 subscribers, benchstat n=8:

  WriteDelay, shrink unset   19.07us -> 12.68us  -33.5% (p=0.010)
                             84 -> 2 allocs/op   -97.6% (p=0.000)
                             34.3KB -> 376B/op   -98.9% (p=0.000)
  WriteDelay, delay tuned    unchanged - no regression where already set
  no WriteDelay (default)    unchanged, ring stays at 2 entries

Deliberately not a capacity floor, which was the first thing I tried. A floor
never gives the memory back: a connection that bursts once at handshake and
then goes quiet would hold it for its whole life, ~900B each, on both the PRO
and the default path. Deferring instead means capacity is held only while the
connection is actually busy and released in full when it goes idle -
TestQueueReclaimsCapacityWhenIdle pins that it returns to 2 entries. Peak
usage is unchanged either way, since the ring has to hold the queued messages
regardless.

Stop server pings from killing the websocket benchmarks mid-run (#602)

BenchmarkWsPubSub, the three BenchmarkWsCommandReplyV2 variants and

Verify Redis PUB/SUB delivery with liveness probes (#594)

* verify Redis PUB/SUB delivery with liveness probes

A PUB/SUB connection can stay healthy on the TCP level while attached
to a Redis node that no longer receives published traffic — after a
Sentinel failover the client may end up on a demoted master, a node
outside the replication chain, or an unrelated Redis on a reused pod
IP (see centrifugal/centrifugo#1189). No connection error ever fires
in that state: the node answers keepalive pings and accepts commands,
publishes keep succeeding, and subscribers starve silently until the
process is restarted.

Verify delivery instead of trusting connection health. Every PUB/SUB
loop counts received messages; when a connection receives nothing for
PubSubProbeInterval (default 30s, negative disables), the loop
publishes a small probe to its service channel through the regular
publish path and expects it back on the connection. One more silent
interval means the connection does not deliver published traffic:
the loop logs a warning, increments a probe_timeout counter and
re-establishes the connection, re-resolving topology.

Probe targets carry no real traffic and are consumed by the loop
itself: the per-shard service channel for broker loops (also SPUBLISH
in sharded mode), and a dedicated per-node channel for the control
loop, whose node channel carries real control commands. In a running
node the control machinery is dormant — node info pings keep that
connection non-idle.

Steady-state cost is one atomic counter increment per received
message. Probes are only sent on idle connections, and any node's
probe delivery suppresses probing on every other subscriber of the
same service channel.

Integration tests cover the failure end to end with real Redis states
only: a replica detached from the master (REPLICAOF NO ONE + SENTINEL
RESET) silently starves the subscriber while publishes succeed, the
probe detects it and the restarted loop re-resolves to the surviving
replica — for both client message and control connections. A disabled
probe baseline documents the old behavior. Idle steady-state tests for
standalone, sharded cluster, map broker and control connections prove
probes rotate correctly, never surface as publications and never fire
false restarts. The docker-compose sentinel service gains two replicas
for these tests.

* restore shared poll key channels after PUB/SUB reconnect

Shared poll subscribes per-key channels at broker level and tracks
them in its own registry — they are not in the Hub. The PUB/SUB loop
resubscribed only Hub().Channels() after re-establishing a connection,
so every reconnect (connection error, failover, liveness probe
restart) silently dropped all key channels at Redis while shared poll
still believed they were subscribed. Key events then never arrived
again on the node until each key was untracked and re-tracked:
live-query push latency degraded to poll cadence, permanently, with
no error anywhere. This existed since key channels were introduced —
any Redis restart triggered it.

Give the resubscribe path a second source: SharedPollManager exposes a
snapshot of the key channels subscribed at a given broker, the Node
surfaces it, and the PUB/SUB loop appends those channels to the Hub
list before the existing per-shard/partition filtering — key channels
are ordinary channels for routing purposes, so the filters apply
unchanged. The map broker does not wire the callback: shared poll
subscribes via node.getBroker, which returns Broker implementations
only, and RedisMapBroker is not one.

The regression test drives the real subscription path
(subscribeToBrokerKeys), kills the PUB/SUB connections through Redis
(CLIENT KILL TYPE pubsub — the same connection error a Redis restart
produces) and requires the key channel to be subscribed and delivering
again once the loop reconnects. Against the Hub-only resubscribe it
fails: the shard service channel comes back, the key channel never
does.

* fixes

Complete subscribe rollback before waking unsubscribe waiters (#608)

commitSubscription's closed-client rollback closed the reservation's
subscribingCh before removing the hub entry. The waiter on that channel
is the unsubscribe loop inside close(): once woken it finds no entry in
c.channels, returns immediately, and close() fires OnDisconnect while the
subscribe goroutine has not yet reached removeSubscription. A caller that
synchronizes on OnDisconnect could therefore observe a hub subscription
belonging to a fully disconnected client, which made
TestClientSubscribingChannelsCleanupOnClientClose flaky in CI.

Do the hub removal (and presence rollback) first and close subscribingCh
last, matching the ordering onSubscribeErrorGen already used. None of the
rollback calls take connectMu or presenceMu, both held by the waiting
close(), so waking later adds no lock-order risk.

Add WebsocketConfig.ProcessCommandsOffReadLoop to cut per-connection memory (#607)

* Add WebsocketConfig.ProcessCommandsOffReadLoop to keep read loop stacks small

A goroutine's stack grows to the deepest call it ever makes and is not given
back while the goroutine lives. A websocket read loop processes commands inline,
so the whole dispatch chain - handler, publish, broker, broadcast fan-out - runs
on it. That has to happen only once, even just the initial connect, for the read
goroutine to reach 8KB and hold it for the connection's entire life, however
idle it becomes afterwards.

When enabled, the read loop hands each frame to a goroutine that exits when the
frame is done. The deep stack returns to the runtime's stack cache and is reused
by whichever connection needs it next, instead of being pinned to one that
spends its life waiting. Measured over 200k idle connections on Linux, the read
loop settles at 4KB instead of 8KB and RSS drops from 22.4KB to 18.4KB per
connection.

Ordering is unchanged: the loop waits for each frame before reading the next.
The handoff is a struct with a method rather than a closure so that no closure is
allocated per frame; only the per-connection struct is.

Off by default, and the trade runs the other way for busy connections: a
goroutine start and two scheduler handoffs per frame is a latency cost, visible
on a connection that sends a command and waits for the reply with nothing else
happening, and absent once many connections are busy at once.

Applied only to the websocket read loop. The SSE, HTTP-stream and emulation
callers of HandleReadFrame run on short-lived request goroutines whose stacks are
released when the request ends, so a handoff there would be pure cost.

Tests cover pipelined ordering, several commands per frame, replies interleaved
with concurrent server pushes, and goroutine cleanup after disconnect.

* Add per-connection footprint benchmarks for the read loop stack

Benchmarks that hold b.N real websocket connections open, put each through
connect/subscribe/publish so its read loop reaches the depth a real connection
reaches, let them go idle, and report what each still occupies. stack-B/conn is
the number ProcessCommandsOffReadLoop is judged on. Also covers the busy case,
where the option was expected to lose and does not, and a probe showing the read
loop's 4KB stack is reached during setup rather than while parsing frames - so
it cannot be reclaimed by restructuring the loop.

Four guards, each of which caught a wrong reading while this was written:

  - commandsPerConn must be >= 1. A connection that never sends a command never
    grows its read loop stack, and both variants would report the same footprint
    while measuring nothing.
  - the server must still hold b.N connections at the end. Server pings had been
    closing connections mid-run, which reported a footprint 25% below the real
    one and looked like a good result.
  - goroutines/conn must be ~1. Anything else means the baseline was taken while
    unrelated goroutines were unwinding, which skews every other metric.
  - a warmup phase before the baseline. A node lazily allocates several MB on
    first use - Prometheus label combinations, summary quantile streams - and
    that fixed cost divided by b.N is larger than the per-connection heap itself.
    It showed up as a +63% heap regression that a profile diff traced entirely to
    centrifuge.New and prometheus.newSummary.

MemStats deltas are taken as signed, since an unsigned wrap renders as a nonsense
3.6e16 rather than an obvious error, and measurements are taken after several GC
cycles because Go shrinks an oversized stack by at most half per cycle.

The load generator needs care and got it wrong first: a publish into a channel
the connection subscribes to produces a reply and a push, and reading only one
leaves the other queued until the server's write queue limit disconnects the
client.

* Cover connection close under the frame handoff

The existing tests close connections from the client side only. That leaves the
one case where the handoff genuinely changes which goroutine does what
unexercised: a close started while a frame is being processed runs on the
handoff goroutine, while the read loop sits in the channel receive waiting for
that same frame.

Two cases, each run against both variants so a divergence shows up rather than
just an absence of failure:

  - a server-side Disconnect while the connection is otherwise quiet, checking
    the read loop is unblocked, the hub drains, and the peer sees the connection
    end;
  - a Disconnect issued from inside an RPC handler, which is the goroutine
    question above. Teardown must complete and must not deadlock against the
    close handshake, which transport close waits on and the read loop is the one
    to drain.

Both pass on either setting, which is what the design predicts: handle() is
synchronous, so no handoff goroutine is ever in flight when the read loop exits,
and the teardown sequence is reached exactly as it was before.

Fix shared poll test deadlock on assertion failure (#609)

Four shared poll tests recorded polled items under a mutex in the
OnSharedPoll handler, but the handler bumped an atomic counter before
taking that mutex. The tests waited on the counter and then asserted on
the recorded items, so a test goroutine that won the race to the mutex
saw an empty slice and failed.

The failure then deadlocked the whole test binary: the assertion ran
while holding the mutex with a plain (non-deferred) Unlock after it, so
require's FailNow -> Goexit left the mutex locked forever. Cleanup then
ran Node.Shutdown -> SharedPollManager.close -> wg.Wait(), waiting on a
refresh worker parked inside the handler on that same mutex. The package
died on the 10m test timeout instead of reporting one failed test.

Assert inside the require.Eventually condition with a deferred unlock
instead. That removes the race (the condition observes the recorded
items, not the counter) and never holds the mutex across a failing
assertion.

Pass a message size limit to the stream command decoder (#612)

* Pass a message size limit to the stream command decoder

Bump github.com/centrifugal/protocol to v0.21.0, which now requires a
positive message size limit when constructing a stream command decoder
(GetStreamCommandDecoder, the unbounded shortcut, was removed). An
unbounded decoder over untrusted input can be driven to allocate
arbitrary memory by a single frame declaring a huge length. See
GHSA-4r3x-2rwr-6w65.

HandleReadFrame now takes a messageSizeLimit and passes it to
GetStreamCommandDecoderLimited, so an oversized declared length is
rejected before it is allocated. Each transport supplies its own limit,
coerced to a positive default:

- WebSocket: MessageSizeLimit, or DecompressedMessageSizeLimit when
  compression is enabled (the decoder sees decoded bytes).
- SSE / HTTP-stream: MaxRequestBodySize.
- Emulation: the length of the already-buffered command bytes, which a
  single command cannot exceed.

All coercions use <= 0 so a negative config cannot reach the decoder.

metrics: add transport_frame_size histogram (#620)

* metrics: add transport_frame_size histogram

Adds a histogram of protocol frame sizes read from client connections,
observed once per frame in HandleReadFrame and labeled by transport.

The existing transport_messages_received and _size counters cannot answer this.
They count individual commands, and a frame may carry many: the protocol
batches, and the SDKs use it - centrifuge-js puts the connect command and every
subscribe into a single frame on each transport open. So dividing those two
counters yields a mean command size, which says nothing about what a frame
weighs, and a ratio of counters has no tail at all.

The tail is the part that matters. WebsocketConfig.MessageSizeLimit is applied
as a transport read limit, so it bounds the whole frame rather than each
command. A client whose batched reconnect frame exceeds it is closed with 1009
on every attempt - already visible after the fact in transport_outgoing_close
_count{code="1009"} - and it is the heaviest users, on the most channels, who
hit it first. This histogram is what lets the limit be chosen from an observed
p99 before that happens, rather than estimated from averages.

Its _count series is the number of frames, so mean commands per frame falls out
of it together with messages_received, without a second metric.

One instrumentation point covers WebSocket, SSE, HTTP stream and emulation,
since all of them read frames through HandleReadFrame. Transports that decode
from a continuous stream have nothing frame-shaped to record and are left alone.

Also exports Node.ObserveTransportFrameSize, mirroring IncTransportOutgoingClose,
so transports implemented outside this package can record frame sizes too.

* metrics: cache the frame size observer per label set

The first version called WithLabelValues on every frame. That hashes and looks
up its label values each time, which is why the per-command transport counters
already cache the resolved metric per label combination - and a frame is just as
much a hot path.

Measured, per frame:

                              before          after
  no client labels        51.7 ns, 0 allocs   33.4 ns, 0 allocs
  with client labels      62.7 ns, 48 B/1     40.0 ns, 8 B/1

For comparison, the existing per-command incTransportMessagesReceived measures
35.0 ns and 51.7 ns for the same two cases, so the frame observation is now
slightly cheaper than one command's counter - and it happens once per frame
rather than once per command.

The remaining 8 B allocation is buildClientLabelsCacheKey constructing the cache
key, shared with the existing counters rather than introduced here.

Adds benchmarks for both, so the comparison stays visible.

Test the Redis presence hash field TTL path (#619)

because CI still ran Redis 6, which has no HEXPIRE. Redis 6 was dropped

Replace the blanket skip with a capability probe: HEXPIRE is attempted

Add TestRedisPresenceManagerWithHashFieldTTLExpire for what the option

sweep. It asserts that refreshing a client extends both its hash field
and its per-user field, that an unrefreshed client disappears, and that

fix client label metrics and Redis payload parsing: wrong series, runtime panics, per-message allocations (#622)

* metrics: key client-label metric caches by the label combination

Four metric emission paths resolve a Prometheus child once and cache it, but
their cache key omitted the client label values while the child was built with
them:

  observeCommandDuration  commandDurationLabels{namespace, frame type}
  incReplyError           replyErrorLabels{frame type, namespace, code}
  incServerDisconnect     disconnectLabels{code}
  incServerUnsubscribe    unsubscribeLabels{code, namespace}

Each of them calls appendClientLabels(baseLabels, c) on a cache miss, so the
child is bound to that one client's label values. With MetricsConfig.ClientLabels
configured, the first client to reach a given (code, namespace, frame type)
combination then owns the child forever: every later client increments the first
client's series regardless of its own labels. One app_region gets all the
traffic and the others report zero.

The transport counters and the frame size histogram already carry a ClientLabels
field in their cache key for exactly this reason. This adds the same field to
the four structs above, filled by a new clientLabelsCacheKey helper that reuses
the key precomputed on the client at connect time, so the hot path stays
allocation free. Nothing changes when ClientLabels is empty (the default): the
key is the empty string.

Adds a regression test that drives all four paths with two clients differing
only in their client label value. Before the fix it reports 2 for app_region=eu
and 0 for app_region=us on the first assertion; after it, both are 1.

Verified with the full package suite against the docker-compose Redis, Valkey
and Dragonfly services, plus go vet and ./internal/....

* metrics: give the remaining client-labeled metrics their label values

recover, recovered_publications and ping_pong_duration_seconds declare
client-label dimensions through buildMetricLabels but passed only the base
label values, so WithLabelValues panicked with an inconsistent cardinality
error as soon as MetricsConfig.ClientLabels was set.

checkPong runs from a time.AfterFunc goroutine, where nothing recovers the
panic, and with the default 25s ping / 10s pong periods the pong deadline
always precedes the next ping - so a node with client labels configured died
about 35 seconds after the first bidirectional client connected. The recover
counters are reached from subscribe handling, which in the default WebSocket
setup runs on the http.Handler goroutine and loses just that connection, but
crashes the process under ProcessCommandsOffReadLoop.

Thread the client through the three call paths and resolve label values with
appendClientLabels, as the other client-labeled metrics do. The ping/pong
observer is now cached per label combination like the transport frame size
one: it runs once per ping interval per connection, and the cache makes it
cheaper than the WithLabelValues call it replaces.

Also key the clientLabelsCacheKey fallback over a full set of empty values, so
a nil client and a client missing every configured label share one cache entry
instead of two entries pointing at the same Prometheus child.

* metrics: stop rebuilding client label keys per message, count subscriptions_accepted

Two more gaps in the client labels feature.

incTransportMessagesReceived and observeTransportFrameSize resolved their
cache key with buildClientLabelsCacheKey on every call, so once ClientLabels
was configured they allocated a string per received command and per read
frame - the two hottest metric paths on the read side. incTransportMessagesSent
already reused the key precomputed on the client at connect time; both now go
through a shared clientLabelValuesAndKey resolver that does the same, and a
test pins all three at zero allocations.

subscriptions_accepted was declared and registered but never incremented, so
it always reported zero. Count it in addSubscription, mirroring how
connections_accepted is counted in addClient: every accepted subscription,
including a resubscribe that overwrites an existing entry, while the inflight
gauge keeps only moving for a genuinely new one.

* metrics: exercise the whole metric surface, validate namespace cache size

The three cardinality panics fixed earlier all shared one cause: nothing ever
called those metrics under a config that enabled client labels. Add a test that
walks every recording path with and without client labels, with a labelled
client and with none, and gathers the registry afterwards, so a metric that
declares dimensions its writer does not fill fails in CI instead of in a
client goroutine.

Also return an error for a ChannelNamespaceCacheSize below -1 instead of
letting the cache constructor panic inside New. -1 remains the documented way
to disable the cache; the neighbouring TTL check already reports its
out-of-range value this way.

* redis: reject malformed PUB/SUB payloads instead of slicing past them

Every length in the Redis publication formats is read off the wire, and the
parsers trusted them. Seven inputs panicked with a slice bounds error:

  extractPushData("__p__x")          [3:1]  - header shorter than the "p1:" tag
  extractPushData("__p1__x")         [3:2]
  parseDeltaPush("d1:1:e:5:abcde")   [6:5]  - prev length leaves no separator
  parseDeltaPush("d1:1:e:-1:x:1:y")  [:-1]  - negative prev payload length
  parseDeltaPush("d1:1:e:1:a:-1:y")  [:-1]  - negative payload length
  parseMessage("d:1:e:-1:x:1:y")     [:-1]  - negative prev length
  parseMessage("d:1:e:1:a:-1:y")     [:-1]  - negative curr length

These run on the PUB/SUB processing goroutine, where nothing recovers, so any
malformed message on a subscribed channel takes the process down - and the same
message is delivered to every node subscribed to it. The data is only as
trustworthy as the Redis instance: a co-tenant publishing to the same keyspace,
a foreign or older publisher, or a corrupted history entry is enough. Malformed
input must be rejected by the caller's existing error path, which is what the
guards restore.

The regression tests live outside the integration build tag - the parsers are
pure functions and need no Redis, but the existing tests for them are tagged and
so never ran in the default suite. Two fuzz targets cover the shape of the bug
rather than the specific inputs; both ran 60s clean (3.2M and 3.3M execs) after
the fix.

* metrics: move the surface test next to the other metric tests

It went into a file of its own when it was written; metrics_test.go is where
the rest of them live.

stress_runtime: cover map subscriptions and shared poll (#623)

The suite had 56 scenarios and none for the two keyed subscription kinds. Both
hand a connection a set of keys rather than a stream of publications, and both
have a handshake nothing else exercises: a map subscription pages through
channel state before it goes live, a shared poll subscription tracks keys that
a server-side refresh loop polls. They are the newest and most concurrent parts
of the library and the only ones the harness could not reach.

Six scenarios:

  map_state_live       state paging delivers every key exactly once, the server
                       flips the reported phase to LIVE on the last page, and
                       updates and removals then arrive live
  map_ttl_removal      keys expiring by KeyTTL are delivered as removals - the
                       cleanup path nothing else drives
  map_churn            connections churning through the whole handshake while
                       keys change underneath leave the hub empty
  shared_poll_track    tracked keys are refreshed at their current version, a
                       removal is delivered, and an untracked key goes quiet
                       while its neighbours keep updating
  shared_poll_churn    subscribe/track/untrack/drop against a 50ms refresh loop
  redis_map_cross_node a key written through node A is in the state a subscriber
                       reads on node B, and updates and removals cross live

Shared poll answers from a harness-owned store (keyed.go), so moving a key's
version there and then seeing the update arrive checks the refresh loop end to
end rather than a mock. Every node gains a map broker - memory on the main node,
Redis on the two Redis nodes, which is what makes the cross-node scenario a
cluster test.

The raw protocol client grew the keyed commands: subscribe carries type, phase,
cursor and limit, and sub_refresh doubles as track/untrack. Its reads also stop
on a caller's condition rather than on a read deadline - letting a deadline
expire fails a gorilla connection for good, so a scenario with commands still to
send must never wait past what it needs.

Send expiration in map subscribe replies, keep client-side refresh across pages (#626)

Map subscriptions stored expireAt and enforced it, but the live subscribe reply
never set expires/ttl, so clients could not refresh the subscription token in
time. Continuation pages of a paginated map subscribe also rebuilt the reply
without ClientSideRefresh, so the committed channel lacked
flagClientSideRefresh and a client sub_refresh was rejected with
DisconnectBadRequest. An already expired map subscription was accepted.

Stream, shared poll and map subscribes now share subscriptionExpiration for the
expires/ttl result fields and the expired check. The map subscribe reservation
keeps ClientSideRefresh for continuation pages, and the first map subscribe
request rejects an already expired subscription with ErrorExpired.

Test the recovery merge gap check and PubSubSync pass-through paths (#624)

MergePublications refuses to merge recovered and buffered publications when
an offset is missing, unless every missing offset belongs to a filtered
publication. That check was not exercised by any test in the repository.
Add cases for a gap with no filtered publications, a gap fully covered by
filtered publications, a gap only partially covered, and overlap between
history and PUB/SUB. Also cover PubSubSync on a channel that is not
buffering, including before StartBuffering and after StopBuffering.

Reject expired client-side subscription refresh (#627)

* Reject expired client-side subscription refresh

handleSubRefresh only rejected a refresh whose ExpireAt was in the past and
never checked SubRefreshReply.Expired. A handler reporting an expired token
with Expired set leaves ExpireAt zero, so the refresh succeeded and stored a
zero expireAt, which disabled expiration for the subscription. Centrifugo
returns exactly this reply when a subscription refresh token has expired.

Check Expired before applying the reply, the same way the server-side
subscription refresh does, and reply with ErrorExpired while keeping the
subscription's existing expiration.

* Reply with ErrorTokenExpired to an expired subscription refresh

A client-side subscription refresh always carries a token, and Expired in
the reply means that token has expired. Reply with ErrorTokenExpired (109)
instead of ErrorExpired (110), the same code an expired token gets on
connect and subscribe, so clients get a new token and retry the refresh
instead of treating the error as final.

* Disconnect with DisconnectSubExpired on an expired subscription refresh

An error reply to sub_refresh is treated as final by some SDKs, which
unsubscribe for good, and before this fix an expired refresh was accepted.
Replying with an error would break integrations that never saw one.

Close the connection with DisconnectSubExpired instead, as an expired
connection refresh closes it with DisconnectExpired. It is a reconnect code:
the client resubscribes, gets ErrorTokenExpired for the old token on
subscribe and requests a new one, which all official SDKs already do. The
close is asynchronous and needs no reply since the connection is gone.

Send full data first after a fossil delta recovery with no publications (#629)

A subscribe with recovery and fossil delta set flagDeltaAllowed whenever
recovery succeeded. When nothing was recovered (the client position was
already the stream top), makeRecoveredPubsDeltaFossil returned no
publications, so no base was sent, yet the next live publication went out
as a delta against the previous stream publication. A client that only
had a stored position, without the data, could not decode it or any
publication after it.

Allow delta at subscribe only if recovered publications were sent. With
nothing recovered, the first live publication is sent with full data and
the write path allows delta after it, as for a subscribe without recovery.

Align fossil deltas to UTF-8 character boundaries for JSON clients (#630)

* Send full data to JSON clients when a fossil delta isn't valid UTF-8

JSON clients get fossil delta data as a JSON string, which can only carry
valid UTF-8. A delta for a change inside a multi-byte character (for example
é to è) contains a lone byte that JSON escaping replaces with U+FFFD, so the
client can't apply the delta and fails with "unknown delta operator".

Send full data instead of such a delta to JSON clients, in live broadcasts,
recovered stream and map publications, and keyed publications.

* Align fossil deltas for JSON clients to UTF-8 character boundaries

A fossil delta for a change inside a multi-byte character splits the
character, which a JSON string can't carry. Sending full data instead turns
delta off for about half of the updates of non-ASCII text.

Rewrite such a delta so its inserts carry whole characters: a boundary inside
a character moves to the character start or end. The output of the delta and
its checksum don't change, so client SDKs need no change.

* Send full data to JSON clients when the delta base isn't valid UTF-8

A JSON client holds data as it arrived in a JSON string, where each byte that
isn't valid UTF-8 became U+FFFD. Every copy of a delta after such a byte points
to the wrong place in the client's data, even if the delta itself is valid
UTF-8. JSON clients get full data unless the previous data is valid UTF-8.

Fix flaky TestRuntimeStability_SlowRefreshHandler (#631)

The refresh handler replied with ExpireAt now+1 in whole seconds. When a
second boundary passed between computing the reply and handling it, the
expiration was already reached and the connection was closed as expired,
failing the test with "connections dropped" (59 of 60). Reply with now+2.
Fix flaky TestPresenceTickDefaultIsAllocationFree (#632)

Don't negotiate delta compression with tags filters (#634)

Delta compression and publication tags filters are documented as mutually
exclusive, but the server negotiated delta for a subscription with a client
tags filter or a server tags filter anyway. To keep the chain of deltas
intact, publications filtered out for such a subscriber were still sent to
it, so the filter wasn't applied.

Delta is now not negotiated for stream and map subscriptions with a tags
filter: they get filtered publications with full data. When a subscription
refresh sets a server tags filter for a stream subscription which negotiated
delta, the subscription is unsubscribed with the insufficient state code and
resubscribes without delta.

Reject map stream reads past an expired stream (#636)

When a map channel's stream expires while its top offset and epoch
survive, a read since an older offset returned an empty page with no
error. Recovery then reported recovered=true and silently skipped the
lost publications, and STREAM phase pagination echoed the same offset
back forever.

Return ErrorUnrecoverablePosition for an empty forward read whose top is
ahead of the requested offset, so clients resync from state.

Scan a payload for UTF-8 validity once per broadcast (#637)

* Scan a payload for UTF-8 validity once per broadcast

JSON clients receive a delta as a JSON string, so they can only be sent
one when the previous payload is valid UTF-8. That check ran inside
createFossilDelta, which a single broadcast reaches once for every
distinct encoding combination among a channel's subscribers, and again
for the broker's and the node's previous publication -- which are
usually the same publication. The same bytes were scanned repeatedly,
and the answer cannot change during a broadcast.

The validity now arrives as a lazyutf8.Validator decided once in
broadcastPublication, so each payload is scanned at most once, and not
at all when no subscriber is a JSON client taking deltas.

It matters only for payloads carrying non-ASCII text. utf8.Valid has an
ASCII fast path, so 16 KiB of ASCII JSON costs around 170ns, while the
same size carrying Cyrillic or emoji costs around 4.5us -- comparable to
building the delta itself. BenchmarkGetDeltaPubUTF8Scan measures both;
on multibyte payloads it is 12% faster for a channel with one encoding
combination, 19% with two and 21% with four, and unchanged on ASCII.

buildPreparedPollData still scans unconditionally. Making that lazy
means deferring the alignment too, which its existing TODO describes and
which is a larger change.

* Keep both benchmark results so neither call is optimised away

* Test that the two previous-payload validators are not swapped

The broker's and the node's previous publications usually share a
validator, so a mis-paired validator would decide a JSON delta on the
wrong payload's UTF-8 validity and stay invisible on the happy path.

A publication with no offset takes the localPrevPub path and skips the
broker delta entirely, so giving the two bases different UTF-8 validity
pins the pairing down end to end. Swapping the arguments in hub.go fails
both subtests.

JSON-encode subscribe reply publications for delta subscriptions (#635)

With fossil delta over the JSON protocol a client gets publication data as
a JSON string: recovered publications and live publications are sent this
way, and SDKs decode the data of such a subscription from a JSON string.
Publications from SubscribeReply were sent with raw data instead, so a JSON
client with negotiated delta failed to decode them. Encode their data as a
JSON string too.

Never block a broadcast on a subscribing client (#640)

A subscription with recovery (or positioning) locked its recovery buffer at the sync point and kept it locked until its result was written. A publication into the channel waited for that buffer while holding the channel's hub shard lock. So anything the subscriber did after the sync point which needed that shard lock deadlocked the node:

A connect with two recoverable channels of one hub shard in ConnectReply.Subscriptions: the second subscription waited for the shard's write lock, and the connect waited for the second subscription.
Client.Subscribe with join/leave and MemoryBroker: the join was published before StopBuffering, and its read lock of the shard queued behind a waiting writer.
After that, everything which needs the shard lock blocks: publications into any of its channels, subscribes, unsubscribes, disconnects and Node.Shutdown.

Even without a deadlock, the lock stalled publications. A connecting client kept the buffers of its connect-time subscriptions locked until all of them were done, including history reads of other channels, and meanwhile every publication into those channels waited, for all their subscribers.

Publications no longer wait for the subscriber (internal/recovery/sync.go).

Before the sync point they are collected and merged into the subscribe result, as before.
After the sync point they are queued.
StopBuffering, called once the result is written, writes the queue in order from the subscriber's goroutine, and then lets publications through.

Use github.com/centrifugal/fdelta for fossil deltas (#638)

Replaces github.com/shadowspore/fossil-delta. Same two functions with the
same signatures, so the swap is the import line; the package is itself
named fdelta, so the alias goes away.

Create is 3.5-4.2x faster on JSON payloads and allocates once instead of
five times -- 128 B/op at 16 KiB against 19 KB. The gap widens on
high-entropy input, where the old encoder's bucket index degenerates:
1 MiB of random bytes takes 343ms there against 17ms here.

Deltas stay byte-compatible in both directions. Clients already deployed
against the old decoder, centrifuge-go among them, apply this encoder's
output unchanged -- checked over 406 payload pairs driven through the
full server path (Create, Align, JSON string encoding) and decoded with
shadowspore/fossil-delta. Delta sizes are identical and no pair lost its
delta: 405 of 406 produce one under either encoder.

_examples keeps shadowspore/fossil-delta as an indirect dependency,
since centrifuge-go still uses it.

Adds BenchmarkCreateFossilDelta, which measures the whole server-side
path -- encoder, UTF-8 alignment and size check -- across payload sizes,
where the existing BenchmarkDeltaFossil only covered a 1.3 KiB fixture.

Limit recovery buffers by ClientQueueMaxSize per connection (#641)

* Limit recovery buffers by ClientQueueMaxSize per connection

Publications buffered while a client subscribes with recovery were limited
by ClientQueueMaxSize per subscribe attempt: a connect with N recoverable
subscriptions could hold about N times the limit while it waited for the
slowest history read. All buffers of a client now share one limit, together
with its write queue, where the buffered publications go.

A publication without offset was written right away once StopBuffering
started, possibly before queued publications published before it. It is
now dropped until the queue is written.

* Count recovery buffers separately from the write queue

The buffers keep sharing one ClientQueueMaxSize limit, but no longer count
the write queue towards it. The subscribe or connect reply, with its
recovered publications, sits in the write queue until it is written: with
the write queue counted, a big recovery result left less room for the
publications queued right after it. A write queue which grows because the
client is slow is limited on its own, and disconnects the client as slow,
not with insufficient state.

It also spares a read lock of the write queue for every buffered
publication.

* Leave room in the write queue in the shared limit test

The publications queued for a connect-time subscription are written after
the connect reply, which may still be in the write queue. With the old
sizes the reply and one channel's publications went over the write queue's
own limit, and the client was disconnected as slow before the overflow of
the buffers could disconnect it with insufficient state.

Split the single-publication Lua scripts into a function and a caller (#642)

broker_history_add_stream.lua and broker_publish_idempotent.lua each did
two things: define what publishing one publication means, and read that
publication out of KEYS and ARGV. Splitting them gives the logic a single
definition and lets the caller name its arguments instead of counting
positions - renumbering ARGV indices by hand when an argument moves is
the failure mode this removes.

The Go side joins the halves back together, so Redis receives the same
self-contained program it always has, and broker_redis_scripts.go is
where that composition lives - which is why broker_redis.go loses two
embeds.

The scripts themselves are unchanged beyond becoming functions: the same
commands in the same order, with the arguments named rather than indexed.
Checked by running the old script and the new one against a real Redis on
identical input and comparing returns, stream contents, meta hash, result
key, TTLs and the published PUB/SUB payloads - 15 cases covering the cache
hit, epoch creation, version accept/suppress/epoch-change, delta with and
without a predecessor, MAXLEN trimming, meta expiry and an empty channel.
All identical.

Centrifugo composes a second, batched caller from the same function half,
which is why one definition is worth more here than two copies that could
drift apart.

Fail an idempotent publish during a slot migration instead of losing it (#644)

With sharded PUB/SUB an idempotent publish without history runs a script
naming one key, the result key. While the slot of its partition migrates,
the node owning the slot does not have a result key which is still to be
written, so Redis redirects the call to the node importing the slot, and
the script runs there. It publishes where the channel has no subscribers -
they stay on the node owning the slot until the migration ends - and
remembers the result. The publish is reported a success, nobody receives
it, and a retry with the same idempotency key is suppressed.

The script now also gets a second key which never exists: the result key
with a suffix, so it always hashes to the same slot. With two keys missing
the importing node answers TRYAGAIN before running anything, so the
publish fails and can be retried. Nothing is remembered, so a retry after
the migration publishes normally.

Only the sharded PUB/SUB path changes. Without it the script publishes
with PUBLISH, which reaches subscribers on every node wherever it runs.

Refuse channels starting with "}" in Redis Cluster; fix idempotent publish with SkipPubSub (#645)

* Report an idempotent publish with SkipPubSub as a success

With SkipPubSub an idempotent publish without history has no channel to
publish to, so its script replies with nothing. Publish passed that nil
reply up as an error although the publication had happened and its
result was remembered: the caller saw a failure, and a retry was
answered from the remembered result.

* Refuse a channel starting with "}" where Redis Cluster keys are tagged by it

In Redis Cluster the broker without sharded PUB/SUB, and the presence
manager, carry the channel as a hash tag in its keys, "{channel}", so
that they share a slot. Redis hashes the text between the first "{" and
the next "}", which for a channel starting with "}" is empty - and then
Redis hashes each whole key instead, putting the keys of one channel in
different slots. Building a call which uses several of them panicked:
publishing with history and reading history in the broker, and presence
calls. The panic happens on the caller's goroutine, so it could take the
process down.

Such a channel is now refused with ErrRedisUnsupportedChannel, which
wraps ErrorBadRequest, so a client asking for it gets a bad request
rather than an internal error. Only those setups are affected: with
single Redis or Sentinel keys have no slots, with sharded PUB/SUB the
broker tags keys by partition, and the map broker always does. A "}"
further into the name is fine, as it ends the tag the same way in every
key of the channel.

* Keep the unsupported channel error unexported

Flush channel batches of all subscribers with one timer per channel (#646)

* Flush channel batches of all subscribers with one timer per channel

With channel batching by delay, every connection subscribed to a channel
started a timer, a channel and a goroutine for each window of the
channel: a publication into a channel with many subscribers started one
per subscriber. The writers of a channel which wait for the same delay
now wait in one batch window, and one timer flushes them all.

Each writer keeps its own buffer and flushes it itself, so what and in
which order a connection receives does not change. A writer flushed for
size stays in its window, and waits no longer than its delay.

1,000 subscribers of a channel, one publication per window: 1,331 -> 80
ns of CPU per subscriber, 2,090 -> 15 allocations per window.
